newsitem.title: USA: It's bonus bonanza time on Wall Street.
newsitem.headline: It's bonus bonanza time on Wall Street.

text.p: Last time, it was cocaine and caviar. This time, it's real estate and savings.

Moneymakers on Wall Street are enjoying their biggest bonus bonanza in years, thanks to a booming 1996, but their taste in spending is tending to practical purchases over luxuries. In the dizzying days a decade ago, tales of decadence abounded. Now Wall Streeters have grown up and calmed down, traders say.

"I haven't heard of anybody buying a lot of cocaine," joked one trader at a Wall Street firm. "And I don't hear people crying that they have $40,000 American Express bills that they have to pay off with their bonuses."

The bonuses are the result of a strong stock market -- the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 26 percent in 1996 -- as well as plenty of mergers, acquisitions and underwriting, said George Wilbanks, managing director of Russell Reynolds Associates, an executive recruiting firm.

Firms such as Morgan Stanley Group Inc., a leader in mergers and acquisitions, said profits rose 26 percent, while at Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc. earnings soared 84 percent. Compensation to top executives, managing directors and partners is up 30, 40 and even 50 percent over the previous year, Wilbanks said.
A RECORD YEAR
"It was a record year," he said.
Investment firms and brokerages will dish out more than $8 billion in bonuses in the first few months of 1997, New York state officials estimate.

Some 1,500 traders, brokers and other Wall Street employees are likely to reap bonuses of $1 million or more, said Alan Johnson, an executive compensation consultant, who estimated that another 100 lucky people will get more than $10 million apiece.
Not all the spending is subdued and sensible, of course. With so many flush with cash, there are still stories of Wall Streeters on spending sprees.

Steven Kessler, owner of a car dealership in midtown Manhattan, tells of three investment firm partners who walked into his showroom on New Year's Eve and left with three brand-new, bright red Ferraris.
"It seems they're getting their bonuses and willing to spend again," said Kessler, whose Ferraris start at $130,000.
JEWELRY, TRAVEL BUSINESS IS BRISK
The jewelry business is brisk at Harry Winston's on Fifth Avenue, a spokeswoman said. "They get their bonus and they tend to spend it," she said of her customers from Wall Street.

And luxury travel is also brisk, thanks in no small part to Wall Street, said Steve Loucks, spokesman for the American Society of Travel Agents in Alexandria, Virginia. "A lot of executives have put off their vacations for a number of years, trying to get through what appeared to be an unsteady economy, and all of a sudden they're going gangbusters with their vacation plans," he said.
But by and large, bonuses are going toward mortgages and savings, especially since many firms are asking employees to take a significant portion in stock rather than cash, Wilbanks said.

And those employees are older and wiser than they once were, he said. "They're gradually realising this isn't a life-long pattern of earning that goes on forever. You're only there five or ten years at the most."
BUYING REAL ESTATE WITH BONUSES

One trader said his bonus-laden colleagues are buying up real estate. "They're into more conservative consumption," he said. "Maybe it's not a car but they'll spend 3 or 4 million on a house. They're being more practical and not as whimsical."
Another said she is seeing more of her co-workers paying off bills or socking the money away. "It's not the same as in past years. Lots of people are a little bit older. Then, they were just kids."

Johnson said he thinks the spending style is a reflection of the times. "It's not as visible. It's not as public," he said. "Being flashy ... is not in tune with the sober '90s. Those kind of excesses were of a different era and a younger generation."
Besides, he added, "with a Ferrari at age 40, you'll probably just hit a telephone pole. Plus you're tired and you just don't go out."
